messages.subject: Hierarchical Dynamic Ordered Probit Regression
parts:
Hi All,

I have been trying to write a Hierarchical Dynamic Ordered Probit Regression. The model features individual- and state-level predictors (all random effects), and time-interactions to add dynamics. Time interactions are drawn from normal priors sharing a variance-term, and all other predictors are drawn from normal priors sharing a variance term. The model does not converge at all, and I assume it has to do with a lack of identifiability because cut-points float and get in the way of the random effects.

I would appreciate any hint to make that model identifiable!

Thanks,
Tobi

data {
  int<lower=0> N;                                         // sample size
  int<lower=2> J;                                         // number of categories
  
  int<lower=0> n_age;                                     // number of age categories
  int<lower=0> n_race;                                    // number of race categories
  int<lower=0> n_edu;                                     // number of education catoegories
  int<lower=0> n_division;                                // number of Divisions
  int<lower=0> n_states;                                  // number of States
  int<lower=0> n_party_id;                                // number of party-categories
  int<lower=0> n_waves;                                   // number of Waves

 
  int<lower=1,upper=n_age> age[N];                        // age for each respondent
  int<lower=1,upper=n_race> race[N];                      // race for each respondent
  int<lower=1,upper=n_edu> edu[N];                        // education for each respondent
  vector<lower=0,upper=1>[N] female;                      // female for each respondent
  int<lower=1,upper=n_party_id> party_id[N];              // party id for each respondent

  int<lower=0,upper=n_states> state[N];                   // state for each respondent
  int<lower=0,upper=n_waves*2> wave_sex[N];               // wave_sex each respondent
  int<lower=0,upper=n_waves*n_age> wave_age[N];           // wave_age for each respondent
  int<lower=0,upper=n_waves*n_edu> wave_edu[N];           // wave_edu for each respondent
  int<lower=0,upper=n_waves*n_race> wave_race[N];         // wave_race for each respondent
  int<lower=0,upper=n_waves*n_party_id> wave_party_id[N]; // wave_party_id for each respondent

 //state level effects
  int<lower=1,upper=n_division> division[n_states];       // division for each state
  real<lower=0,upper=100> vote_prev_state[n_states];      // 2012 vote at the state-level

  int<lower=1,upper=J> y[N];                              // vote-choice
                                                            
}
parameters {
 real beta;                                               // common intercept
  real sex;                                               // female slope                    
  vector[n_age] a_age;                                    // age random effects
  vector[n_edu] a_edu;                                    // education random effects
  vector[n_race] a_race;                                  // race random effects
  vector[n_party_id] a_party_id;                          // party random effects
  vector[n_waves*2] a_wave_sex;                           // change for female                    
  vector[n_waves*n_age] a_wave_age;                       // change for sex
  vector[n_waves*n_edu] a_wave_edu;                        // change for edu
  vector[n_waves*n_race] a_wave_race;                      // change for race
  vector[n_waves*n_party_id] a_wave_party_id;              // change for party

                                                          //state level effects
  vector[n_division] a_division;                          // division random effects
  real gamma;                                             // previous vote- slope
  vector [n_states] a_state;                              // state effects
  ordered[J-1] tau;                                       // thresholds
  
  
                                                          // sigmas
  real<lower=0,upper=100> sigma;                          // sd for base-line parameters  
  real<lower=0,upper=100> sigma_change;                   // sd for dynamic parameters  
}


transformed parameters{                                   // state-level effects transformed
  real a_state_hat [n_states];
  for (s in 1:n_states)
a_state_hat[s]<-a_division[division[s]]+gamma*vote_prev_state[s];
}

model {
  vector[J] theta;
sigma ~ cauchy(0,2.5);                                    // half-cauchy priors, p. 54 for reference
sigma_change ~ cauchy(0,2.5);

a_age ~ normal (0, sigma);                                //base-line parameters
a_edu ~ normal (0, sigma);
a_race ~ normal (0, sigma);
a_party_id ~ normal (0, sigma);
beta ~ normal(0, sigma);
sex ~ normal(0, sigma);

gamma ~ normal(0, sigma);
a_division ~ normal (0, sigma);

a_wave_sex~ normal (0, sigma_change);                   //change parameters
a_wave_age~ normal (0, sigma_change);
a_wave_edu~ normal (0, sigma_change);
a_wave_race~ normal (0, sigma_change);
a_wave_party_id~ normal (0, sigma_change);

                                                       //#1st Level
a_state~ normal(a_state_hat,sigma);


for (i in 1:N) {                                      //Log Likelihood
real y_hat;
y_hat <- beta + sex * female[i]+a_state[state[i]]+
a_party_id[party_id[i]] + a_age[age[i]]+a_edu[edu[i]] + a_race[race[i]]+
+a_wave_sex[wave_sex[i]]+a_wave_age[wave_age[i]]+a_wave_edu[wave_edu[i]]+a_wave_race[wave_race[i]]+a_wave_party_id[wave_party_id[i]];
theta[1] <- 1 - Phi(y_hat - tau[1]);
for (k in 2:(J-1))
theta[k] <- Phi(y_hat - tau[k-1]) - Phi(y_hat - tau[k]);
theta[J] <- Phi(y_hat - tau[J-1]);
y[i] ~ categorical(theta);
} }

You could also try doing the same thing with the other
varying intercepts ("random effects") as with sex, that
is use only (A - 1) of the A possibilities and set the other
one to 0. The models aren't identified other than through
priors otherwise.

Also, I'm not sure why you use the same hierarchical scales
sigma and sigma_change everywhere. Don't you expect the scale
of effects to vary?

Given that you're setting the first cutpoint to 0, you
probably want the rest of them to be positive,
so rather than

ordered[J-2] tau_raw;

you probably want

positive_ordered[J - 2] tau;

which ensures all tau[j] > 0.

I just defined tau directly. We won't need tau_raw, but can
just define the cumulative probabilty terms so that the calls
to Phi aren't repeated:

vector[J] phi_cumulative;
phi_cumulative[j] <- Phi(y_hat); // tau[1] = 0 by construction
for (j in 2:(J - 1))
phi_cumulative[j] <- Phi(y_hat - tau[j - 1]);
phi_cumulative[J] <- 1;

Then I'd use those to define theta:

theta[1] <- phi_cumulative[1];
for (j in 2:J)
theta[j] <- phi_cumulative[j] - phi_cumulative[j - 1];

It'll be much more efficient without the repeated calls to Phi
and there's some savings from not having to write out two versions
of tau. You could shave a little more off by defining theta[J] directly
and making phi_cumulative size J - 1 in stead of J, but that probably won't
be noticeable.

I'd also suggest writing the linear predictor as

<- beta
+ sex * female[i]
+ a_state[state[i]]

+ a_party_id[party_id[i]]
+ a_age[age[i]]

R and BUGS and JAGS make you write + at the end of a line because
they have parsers that treat end-of-line whitespace differently
than other whitespace, but start of line is traditional in code
and in math typesetting.

Hi All.

I have been playing around with the dynamic model for a long time. It turns out that using weakly informative priors as specified by Gelman (2008) to anchor the dynamic parameters helps; I also had to tweak the max_treedepth, but now the model converges beautifully, and has some of the desired properties (i.e. strong correlation between beta_t and beta_(t-1) that wears off slowly deeper down the temporal chain (model below). 

Two problems remain: 

First, my division random effects have a very wide posterior distribution for divisions in which I have no data (specifically, Division 3 and Division 6; I can post posterior results if desired). From my understanding, the posterior here should be pretty much the same as the prior, i.e. have 95% of the probability mass between -0.9 and 0.9, but the estimated standard deviation is >10. 

Second, I am trying to use the model results to get probability estimates for voting for specific demographic combinations, but I am unsure what metric to use to construct point estimates and credible intervals. My initial idea was to construct HPD intervals by doing something like  

 params_dem<-extract(fit)
best_dem<-which.max(params_dem$lp__)

and do the same for the 2.5% and 97.5% percentile. The problem here is that different model runs yield very different point estimates, which I guess is attributable to the built-in strong correlative structure of the model. I guess alternatively I can construct n.draws probability estimates for each demographic combination and then take the empirical percentiles, but even this yields substantively different point estimates. Having said that, the model converges perfectly in terms of the Rubin-Gelman diagnostic. I can't quite wrap my head around this, and any suggestions as to how to construct reliable point-estimates of probability and credible intervals based on the below model are more than welcome!

Many thanks again,
Tobi

parts:
Extreme quantiles, including min and max, are extremely noisy.  Stick
to at least 5/95, if not 10/90, to get more stable results.

On Apr 5, 2016, at 4:43 PM, Tobias Konitzer <tobias....@gmail.com> wrote:

Second, I am trying to use the model results to get probability estimates for voting for specific demographic combinations, but I am unsure what metric to use to construct point estimates and credible intervals. My initial idea was to construct HPD intervals by doing something like  

 params_dem<-extract(fit)
best_dem<-which.max(params_dem$lp__)

and do the same for the 2.5% and 97.5% percentile. The problem here is that different model runs yield very different point estimates, which I guess is attributable to the built-in strong correlative structure of the model. I guess alternatively I can construct n.draws probability estimates for each demographic combination and then take the empirical percentiles, but even this yields substantively different point estimates. Having said that, the model converges perfectly in terms of the Rubin-Gelman diagnostic. I can't quite wrap my head around this, and any suggestions as to how to construct reliable point-estimates of probability and credible intervals based on the below model are more than welcome!

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Re: 2.5%/97.5% intervals are generally a bad idea
parts:
I'm not sure what Andrew's thinking, but part of the problem
is computational --- you need a lot of draws to estimate tail
quantiles (you can think of this as only 2.5% of the samples
coming into play to help estimate the lower bound of a 95%
interval).

Another issue is that tails can be more sensitive to priors
than central intervals or posterior means.

You can see all this through simulation by rerunning with different
seeds and different priors and looking at variance in the 2.5%
vs. 50% quantile estimates. More things to go in the book!

- Bob

parts:
Hi, beyond the computational issue, my argument is that for decision making we want to know roughly where the parameter is but there’s no need to be requiring 97.5% certainty or anytihng close to that. Of course in prediction problems we might care about things like 100-year floods, but for basic parameter esitmation it seems to me that 50% intervals make more sense. Depends on context, of course, and I’ve struggled to figure out exactly how to write this up (even for blog, let alone in a paper or book).
A
